Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls you in the middle of the night, crying, because they just received some devastating family news.
Expectation2: Perform maintenance and cleaning of the machines to ensure optimal performance
Situation2: Routine servicing is scheduled next week during a planned shutdown.
Story: It was 2 a.m. when my phone buzzed, jolting me awake. On the other end, my friend’s voice trembled, words tumbling out between sobs about a family emergency. I sat up, heart pounding, trying to listen, to be present, to offer the comfort they so desperately needed. But as I murmured reassurances, my mind kept drifting to the maintenance schedule taped above my desk. The planned shutdown was next week, and I was already behind on prepping the machines. If I didn’t get a head start, I’d risk missing the narrow window for servicing, and any delay could mean costly downtime for the whole plant. My friend’s pain pulled at me, demanding my empathy and time, while the looming responsibility of my job pressed in, reminding me of the trust my team placed in me. I gripped the phone tighter, torn between the urge to stay on the line and the nagging anxiety about the work piling up. The weight of both roles pressed down, and I felt myself caught in the middle, unable to fully be the friend or the repairer I was expected to be.
